title: Molinaeus: fiducia is faith’s inseparable fruit — hope, security, quiet joy
source_text: LXXII. Caeterum ab ea persuasione distinguit fiduciam, quae ex illa oritur, & quam vult esse fidei justificantis perpetuam comitem, nec fidem ipsam, sed fidei effectum, sine quo non est vera fides. Per fiduciam enim intelligit spem firmam, & animi quandam constantiam, securitatem, & tranquillitatem; oppositam terrori & trepidationi, per quam, ut verbis ejus utar, terrores excutiuntur, & voluntas placida pace componitur, & laetitia perfunditur, & fidelis Deum familiariter & multa cum libertate compellat. Censeo, inquit, aliud esse fidem, aliud fiduciam. Hanc esse illius fructum & effectum inseparabilem. Nam simulac mens firmo assensu credidit promissiones Evangelii ad se pertinere, illico terrores excutiuntur, & voluntas placida pace componitur, & laetitia perfunditur; per quam fit ut animus plenus fiducia, docente Spiritu adoptionis, Deum familiariter, multaque cum libertate compellat. De Justit. & Fide justific. parte 2. Thesi 19.
pass_a_gloss: But further, he distinguishes from that persuasion the trust which arises from it, and which he wants to be the perpetual companion of justifying faith — not faith itself, but an effect of faith, without which there is no true faith. For by trust he understands a firm hope, and a certain constancy of mind, security, and tranquillity; opposed to terror and trembling, by which, to use his words, terrors are shaken off, and the will is composed with quiet peace, and joy is poured abroad, and the believer addresses God familiarly and with much liberty. I judge, he says, that faith is one thing, trust another. That this is its fruit and inseparable effect. For as soon as the mind with firm assent has believed that the promises of the Gospel pertain to itself, immediately terrors are shaken off, and the will is composed with quiet peace, and joy is poured abroad; whereby it comes to pass that the mind full of trust, the Spirit of adoption teaching, addresses God familiarly and with much liberty. On Justification and Justifying Faith, part 2, Thesis 19.
pass_b_english: Du Moulin sets fiducia apart from that persuasion: fiducia rises from it as justifying faith’s perpetual companion — not faith itself, but faith’s effect, without which faith is not true.
Fiducia = firm hope, constancy, security, tranquillity against terror and trembling.
In his words: terrors shaken off, will quieted in peace, joy poured out, the believer calling on God with familiar liberty.
Faith is one thing, fiducia another — its inseparable fruit: once the mind firmly assents that Gospel promises are for me, that quiet joy follows by the Spirit of adoption.
